title: Slope and Average Rate of Change
learningObjective: Determine the average rate of change of a given function over a given interval. Find the slope of a line.

faqs.question: What is average rate of change, and what does it actually measure?
faqs.answer: Average rate of change measures how much a function's output changes, on average, per unit of input, over a specific interval. Think of it like a road trip: if you drove 120 miles in 2 hours, your average speed was 60 mph — that doesn't mean you drove exactly 60 mph the whole time, just that on average, that's your rate. Average rate of change works the same way: it tells you the overall trend across an interval, not the behavior at every single instant.

faqs.question: What is the formula for average rate of change, and what do the parts mean?
faqs.answer:
The formula compares how much the output changed to how much the input changed, over the interval [a, b], where a < b.
Formula

\[ \text{Average Rate of Change} = \dfrac{f(b)-f(a)}{b-a} \]

\( f(b) \) and \( f(a) \) are the y-values (outputs) at the two ends of the interval. \( b \) and \( a \) are the x-values (inputs). The numerator is the change in output; the denominator is the change in input.

faqs.question: What is slope, and how does it relate to average rate of change?
faqs.answer: Slope is a constant number that describes the steepness and direction of a non-vertical line (a vertical line has no slope; see the FAQ on horizontal and vertical lines). For a linear function specifically, the average rate of change is always the same no matter which interval you pick — and that constant value is exactly what we call the slope. In other words: slope is just the average rate of change of a linear function, and it never changes.

faqs.question: Why does a linear function have a constant rate of change, but other functions don't?
faqs.answer:
A straight line rises (or falls) at exactly the same steepness everywhere along it — that's what makes it "straight." A curve, on the other hand, bends, so its steepness changes as you move along it — steeper in some places, flatter in others.

Left: on a line, every run of 3 gives the same rise. Right: on this curve, a run of 3 gives a small rise on the left and a big rise on the right, so the curve gets steeper as you move right.

faqs.question: What does it mean for slope to be positive or negative?
faqs.answer:
The sign of the slope tells you the direction of the line, reading left to right. A positive slope means the line rises as you move right — the function is increasing. A negative slope means the line falls as you move right — the function is decreasing. The size of the number (ignoring the sign) tells you the steepness; the sign alone tells you the direction.

Reading left to right: the left line climbs (positive slope); the right line falls (negative slope).

faqs.question: What is the slope formula, and where does it come from?
faqs.answer:
The slope formula is just the average rate of change formula, rewritten using point notation instead of function notation — same idea, different labels.
Formula

Given two points \( (x_1, y_1) \) and \( (x_2, y_2) \):

\[ m = \dfrac{y_2 - y_1}{x_2 - x_1} \]

This works when \( x_1 \ne x_2 \). If the two x-values are equal, the line is vertical and its slope is undefined.

This is "change in y" over "change in x" — or, informally, rise over run.

faqs.question: Extension: How do I calculate average rate of change from a table of values?
faqs.answer:
This goes beyond the LF1 CheckIt exercise, where the function is always given as a formula. Pick your two endpoints from the table, and plug their x- and y-values into the average rate of change formula. You don't need any points in between — only the two endpoints of your interval matter.
Worked Example

Table: (−5, 28), (−4, 19), (−3, 12), (−2, 7)

Find the average rate of change from \( x=-5 \) to \( x=-2 \):

\[ \dfrac{f(-2)-f(-5)}{-2-(-5)} = \dfrac{7-28}{3} = \dfrac{-21}{3} = -7 \]

faqs.question: Extension: How do I calculate average rate of change from a graph?
faqs.answer:
This goes beyond the LF1 CheckIt exercise, where the function is always given as a formula. Identify the two x-values that define your interval, find their corresponding y-values on the graph, then apply the formula exactly as you would with a table — the graph is just showing you the same (x, y) pairs visually.

Mark your two endpoints, then find the vertical distance (rise) and horizontal distance (run) between them.

faqs.question: How do I calculate average rate of change when I'm only given an equation?
faqs.answer:
Evaluate the function at both endpoints of the interval to get your two y-values, then plug everything into the formula — this is the average rate of change formula in action.
Worked Example

Let \( f(x) = -3x^2 - 1 \). Find the average rate of change on \( [-2, 3] \).

\( f(-2) = -3(-2)^2-1 = -13 \)

\( f(3) = -3(3)^2-1 = -28 \)

\[ \dfrac{f(3)-f(-2)}{3-(-2)} = \dfrac{-28-(-13)}{5} = \dfrac{-15}{5} = -3 \]

faqs.question: Why do I get a different average rate of change depending on which interval I pick (for non-linear functions)?
faqs.answer: Because a curved graph's steepness genuinely changes from place to place, the "average steepness" you calculate depends entirely on which two points you choose. The average rate depends only on the two endpoint outputs, so rises and falls inside the interval can cancel: \( f(x)=x^2 \) has average rate 0 on \( [-2,2] \) even though it changes a lot inside. Different intervals usually give different average rates, but two intervals can also happen to give the same one. This is completely expected for anything that isn't a straight line — it's actually one of the key differences between linear and non-linear functions.

faqs.question: Which point is (x₁, y₁) and which is (x₂, y₂) in the slope formula — does it matter?
faqs.answer:
It doesn't matter which point you call "first" and which you call "second" — but you do have to stay consistent within the same calculation. Whichever point you subtract first in the numerator, you must subtract that same point first in the denominator too. Swap both, and you'll get the exact same slope; swap just one, and you'll flip the sign by mistake.
Worked Example

Points: \( (-3, 7) \) and \( (7, 2) \)

Either order works: \( \dfrac{2-7}{7-(-3)} = \dfrac{-5}{10} = -\dfrac{1}{2} \)

or \( \dfrac{7-2}{-3-7} = \dfrac{5}{-10} = -\dfrac{1}{2} \) — same answer either way.

faqs.question: Why is the slope of a horizontal line 0, but the slope of a vertical line undefined?
faqs.answer:
A horizontal line has zero rise — the y-values never change — so for any two different points the numerator is 0 and the denominator is not, and 0 divided by a nonzero number is 0. A vertical line has zero run — the x-values never change — so the denominator becomes 0, and division by zero is undefined. That's not a technicality; it reflects something real: a vertical line doesn't have a single steepness value at all. (CheckIt's LF1 lines are never vertical, but a slope of 0 can come up.)

Horizontal line (left): zero vertical change. Vertical line (right): zero horizontal change — division by zero.

faqs.question: What's the difference between "rise over run" and the slope formula — are they the same thing?
faqs.answer: They're the same idea, just two different ways to say it. "Rise over run" is the informal, visual version — count squares up/down and left/right on a graph (counting down or left counts as negative). The slope formula, m = (y₂ − y₁)/(x₂ − x₁), is the precise algebraic version — it works even when you can't easily count grid squares, like when coordinates are fractions or decimals.

faqs.question: Extension: How do I interpret slope in a real-world context?
faqs.answer: This goes beyond the LF1 CheckIt exercise, which asks only for numbers. In context, slope tells you how much the output changes per unit of input — often per unit of time. If a room's temperature has an average rate of change of −0.7 °F per minute over a 10-minute interval, the temperature dropped 7 °F in those 10 minutes, about seven-tenths of a degree per minute on average. If the temperature is modeled by a line, it drops exactly 0.7 °F every minute. The sign gives the direction and the size gives how fast; always attach units, written as output units per input unit.

faqs.question: How does average rate of change here connect to what we'll see later with functions in general?
faqs.answer: Average rate of change is a tool you'll apply to every family of function you study from here on — polynomial, rational, exponential, trigonometric. Linear functions are simply the easiest case, since the rate of change never changes. As you move to more complex functions, you'll use this exact same formula to describe how fast they're growing or shrinking over any interval you choose.

faqs.question: Extension: Why does slope matter beyond just lines — where will this come back later in the course?
faqs.answer: Slope is your first exposure to one of the biggest ideas in all of mathematics: measuring how fast something changes. Later in calculus, this exact concept becomes the derivative — the instantaneous rate of change at a single point, rather than the average over an interval. Everything you're learning now about rise over run and average rate of change is quietly laying the foundation for that idea.

guided.title: Grade a Classmate's Average Rates of Change
guided.prompt: I'm practicing LF1 in Math 172: the average rate of change of f on an interval [a, b], which is (f(b) − f(a))/(b − a). My CheckIt exercise uses three kinds of function: a polynomial of degree 2, 3 or 4 with up to three terms, like 2x^3 − x + 4; a square root like sqrt(3x + 1); or a fraction like (2x − 3)/(x + 2). The interval has integer endpoints that are 2 to 6 apart. Answers are exact: fractions stay fractions and roots stay roots. CheckIt sometimes prints a root answer split up, like -1/4*sqrt(7) + 1/4*sqrt(19), which equals (sqrt(19) − sqrt(7))/4. Play a classmate. Give me three problems, one of each kind, and show only your final answers, not your work. For the square root, choose numbers so that the inside is positive at both endpoints and at least one expression inside the square root works out to a positive integer that is not a perfect square, so the answer is irrational. For the fraction, choose an interval where the bottom is never 0. Make exactly one of your three answers wrong in a realistic way: treating (−2)^4 as −16, dividing by b instead of b − a, combining sqrt(19) − sqrt(7) into sqrt(12), or subtracting the outputs in one order and the inputs in the other. Don't tell me which one. I'll work all three problems myself and compare. For an answer with a root, I'll also compare calculator decimals, since an exact answer and its split form give the same decimal. Then I'll name the wrong answer and fix it. After I respond, check my reasoning and give me the fully corrected solution before we finish.

guided.title: Why a Line's Rate Never Changes
guided.prompt: I'm learning in Math 172 (LF1) that a line has the same average rate of change on every interval, and that this number is its slope, but a curve's average rate of change depends on the interval. Use the line y = 3x − 2 and the quadratic f(x) = x^2 − 4x + 1, and the intervals [0, 2] and [3, 5]. Don't compute anything yet. First ask me to predict whether the line's two average rates of change will match, and whether the quadratic's will. Then let me compute all four, one at a time, with (f(b) − f(a))/(b − a). Ask a short question if I get stuck, but don't do the arithmetic for me. Next, ask me to explain, using the shape of each graph, why the quadratic's two numbers differ even though both intervals have length 2. Finally, write a 3-sentence summary of the pattern with exactly one deliberate mistake in it, such as claiming the quadratic's rate is the same on any two intervals of the same length, or that the line's rate depends on which two points you pick. I'll find the mistake by checking it against my four numbers. After I respond, check my reasoning and give me the fully corrected solution before we finish.

guided.title: Slope from Points and Tables
guided.prompt: I'm practicing LF1 in Math 172: the slope of a line from two points or from a table, m = (y2 − y1)/(x2 − x1). On CheckIt, one of these two slopes is an integer (it can be 0) and the other is a fraction like 13/4 or −7/3, written as a reduced fraction, proper or improper (not a mixed number). The table runs down the page as an x column and a y column, and its x-values are not evenly spaced. Give me four problems, one at a time: (1) two integer points with a integer slope; (2) two integer points with a fraction slope (reduced, proper or improper) whose denominator is 2, 3, 4 or 5; (3) a 5-row x | y table with unevenly spaced integer x-values and a fraction slope; (4) a table or pair of points whose slope is 0. Before I calculate each one, ask me to predict the sign from how y changes as x increases. Don't give me answers. If I'm wrong, ask a question that points to the step. After problem 4, show me your own solution to a new table problem with one deliberate mistake, such as subtracting in different orders on the top and bottom, or using the change in y between two rows as if x went up by 1. I'll find it by redoing the slope with a different pair of rows. After I respond, check my reasoning and give me the fully corrected solution before we finish.

guided.title: Grade a Classmate's Three Slopes
guided.prompt: I'm practicing LF1 in Math 172. CheckIt asks for the slope of three lines: one graphed on a −10 to 10 grid with no points marked (its slope is a multiple of 1/2 from −3 to 3, and can be 0), one given by an x | y table of 4 to 6 rows with unevenly spaced x-values, and one through two points. Play a classmate who has just finished one of these sets. For the graphed line, you can't show me a picture, so describe it by three grid corners it passes through, listed out of order. Show me only your three final slopes, and make exactly one of them wrong in a realistic way: run over rise, the wrong sign for the direction the line goes, the y-intercept given as the slope, or the change in y between two table rows used without dividing by the change in x. Don't tell me which one is wrong. I'll compute each slope myself; for the graph, I'll plot the three corners on graph paper and count the rise and run between two of them. Then I'll name the wrong answer and explain the fix. Write all math as plain text. After I respond, check my reasoning and give me the fully corrected solution before we finish.

guided.title: Extension: From Average Rate to Instantaneous Rate
guided.prompt: This goes beyond the LF1 CheckIt exercise. I know how to find the average rate of change of f on [a, b] with (f(b) − f(a))/(b − a), and I've heard that calculus uses this idea to find how fast a function changes at a single instant. Use f(x) = x^2 and the point x = 1. Ask me to compute the average rate of change on [1, 2], then [1, 1.5], then [1, 1.1], then [1, 1.01], one at a time, and don't compute them for me. Then ask me to predict what number the results are approaching, and what that number might mean on the graph of y = x^2 at the point (1, 1). After I answer, explain the connection to the derivative in 3 or 4 plain sentences with no calculus notation, and include one deliberate mistake, such as saying the results approach 1, or that the line through the two points gets steeper as the interval shrinks. I'll check your explanation against my four numbers. After I respond, check my reasoning and give me the fully corrected solution before we finish.

paths.label: LF1: Slope and Average Rate of Change
paths.sectionLabel: LF1, Slope and Average Rate of Change
paths.intro: Builds to the LF1 check: finding an average rate of change, and finding slopes of lines given as a graph, a table, or two points. Practice scope: the path uses CheckIt's three kinds of function for average rate of change (polynomials of degree 2 to 4, square roots like \(\sqrt{3x+1}\), and fractions like \(\dfrac{x+3}{x-1}\)) on intervals with integer endpoints, with exact answers (leave roots and fractions as they are); lines graphed on CheckIt's −10 to 10 grid with no points marked; and tables written as an x column and a y column whose x-values are not evenly spaced. Vertical lines, average rate of change from a table or graph, and the Extension FAQs and videos go beyond the LF1 CheckIt exercise and are optional.

stages.desc: Two quick skills LF1 leans on. Skip any you already have.

stops.title: Evaluate roots and fractions
stops.target: Evaluate a function with a square root or a fraction at a given input.
stops.coldPlain: Let f(x) = sqrt(2x + 9). Find f(8) and f(0).
stops.solution: f(8) = sqrt(2(8) + 9) = sqrt(25) = 5. f(0) = sqrt(0 + 9) = sqrt(9) = 3. Simplify inside the root first.
stops.mistake: Taking the square root of each term separately, like sqrt(2x) + sqrt(9).
stops.reflect: What do you simplify first when there is a root or a fraction bar?

stops.title: Simplify a fraction of differences
stops.target: Simplify a fraction of differences like \(\dfrac{-3 - 5}{2 - (-4)}\), keeping track of negatives.
stops.solution: Top: -3 - 5 = -8. Bottom: 2 - (-4) = 2 + 4 = 6. So -8/6 = -4/3 after dividing top and bottom by 2.
stops.mistake: Turning 2 - (-4) into -2, or forgetting to reduce the fraction.
stops.reflect: What does subtracting a negative turn into?

stages.desc: One stop per type of question on the LF1 check.

stops.title: Slope from two points
stops.target: Find the slope of the line through two points using \(m = \dfrac{y_2 - y_1}{x_2 - x_1}\).
stops.cold: Find the slope of the line through \((-3, 8)\) and \((1, -8)\).
stops.coldPlain: Find the slope of the line through (-3, 8) and (1, -8).
stops.mistake: Subtracting in a different order on the top and bottom, or putting the x-values on top.
stops.note: If you give me another problem, use integer points and make the slope a whole number or an improper fraction like -7/4, the kinds CheckIt uses.
stops.again: Find the slope of the line through \((5, -6)\) and \((-3, 8)\).
stops.againA: \(m = \dfrac{8 - (-6)}{-3 - 5} = \dfrac{14}{-8} = -\dfrac{7}{4}\). Leave it as an improper fraction.
stops.reflect: Why does the order of subtraction have to match on the top and bottom?

stops.title: Slope from a table
stops.target: Find the slope of a line from a table by choosing any two rows and using the slope formula.
stops.cold:
Find the slope of the line defined by this table.
\(x\)\(y\)
\(-3\)\(-7\)
\(-1\)\(-1\)
\(2\)\(8\)
\(6\)\(20\)
stops.coldPlain: Find the slope of the line defined by this table. x | y rows: (-3, -7), (-1, -1), (2, 8), (6, 20)
stops.coldA: \(3\). Using the first two rows: \(\dfrac{-1 - (-7)}{-1 - (-3)} = \dfrac{6}{2} = 3\). Any two rows give the same answer.
stops.solution: Pick any two rows, for example (-3, -7) and (-1, -1): m = (-1 - (-7))/(-1 - (-3)) = 6/2 = 3. Checking another pair, (2, 8) and (6, 20): 12/4 = 3.
stops.mistake: Using the change in y between rows without dividing by the change in x (the x-values are not evenly spaced).
stops.note: My table runs down the page as an x column and a y column, and its x-values are not evenly spaced. If you give me another table, do the same.
stops.again:
Find the slope of the line defined by this table.
\(x\)\(y\)
\(-6\)\(8\)
\(-3\)\(6\)
\(3\)\(2\)
\(9\)\(-2\)
stops.reflect: Why can you pick any two rows of the table?

stops.title: Slope from a graph
stops.target: Find the slope of a graphed line by finding two points where it crosses grid corners, then computing rise over run.
stops.cold: Find the slope of the line graphed below.[[graph:LA]]
stops.coldPlain: Find the slope of the line in the graph.
stops.graphNote: The graph is a straight line on a -10 to 10 grid, with no points marked, crossing the grid corners (-2, -7), (0, -3) and (2, 1).
stops.coldA: \(2\). For example, from \((0, -3)\) to \((2, 1)\), the line rises 4 while running 2, and \(\tfrac{4}{2} = 2\).
stops.solution: Find two points where the line crosses grid corners exactly, such as (0, -3) and (2, 1). Rise = 1 - (-3) = 4, run = 2 - 0 = 2. Slope = 4/2 = 2.
stops.mistake: Reading points that are not exactly on grid corners, or counting run as rise.
stops.note: For the similar problem, you can't draw, so tell me the y-intercept and one other grid corner on a -10 to 10 grid, and I'll sketch it. Use a slope that is a multiple of 1/2 from -3 to 3.
stops.again: Find the slope of the line graphed below.[[graph:LB]]
stops.againA: \(-\dfrac{3}{2}\). For example, from \((0, 1)\) to \((2, -2)\): down 3, right 2.
stops.reflect: What makes a point a good one to read from a graph?

stops.title: Average rate of change
stops.target: Find the average rate of change of \(f\) on \([a, b]\): \(\dfrac{f(b) - f(a)}{b - a}\), the slope between two points on the graph.
stops.cold: Find the average rate of change of \(f(x) = x^4 - 3x^2\) on the interval \([-1, 3]\).
stops.coldPlain: Find the average rate of change of f(x) = x^4 - 3x^2 on the interval [-1, 3].
stops.mistake: Treating (-1)^4 or (-1)^2 as negative, or dividing by 3 (the right endpoint) instead of 3 - (-1) = 4.
stops.note: If you give me another problem, use a polynomial of degree 2, 3 or 4 with up to three terms, on an interval with integer endpoints that are 2 to 6 apart.
stops.again: Find the average rate of change of \(g(x) = -2x^3 + x\) on \([-1, 2]\).
stops.reflect: How is average rate of change the same idea as slope?

stops.title: Average rate of change with roots and fractions
stops.target: Find the average rate of change when the function has a square root or a fraction.
stops.cold: Find the average rate of change of \(f(x) = \sqrt{3x + 1}\) on \([2, 6]\).
stops.coldPlain: Find the average rate of change of f(x) = sqrt(3x + 1) on [2, 6].
stops.coldA: \(f(6) = \sqrt{19}\) and \(f(2) = \sqrt{7}\); neither simplifies. So \(\dfrac{\sqrt{19} - \sqrt{7}}{6 - 2} = \dfrac{\sqrt{19} - \sqrt{7}}{4}\). Leave it exact. CheckIt may print it as \(-\tfrac{1}{4}\sqrt{7} + \tfrac{1}{4}\sqrt{19}\), which is the same number (about 0.428).
stops.solution: f(6) = sqrt(18 + 1) = sqrt(19) and f(2) = sqrt(6 + 1) = sqrt(7). Average rate of change = (sqrt(19) - sqrt(7))/(6 - 2) = (sqrt(19) - sqrt(7))/4. sqrt(19) - sqrt(7) is not sqrt(12): roots do not subtract that way. CheckIt may write the answer as -1/4*sqrt(7) + 1/4*sqrt(19).
stops.mistake: Combining sqrt(19) - sqrt(7) into sqrt(19 - 7) = sqrt(12), or turning the exact answer into a rounded decimal.
stops.note: Keep answers exact. CheckIt may print a root answer split up, like -1/4*sqrt(7) + 1/4*sqrt(19), which equals (sqrt(19) - sqrt(7))/4.
stops.again: Find the average rate of change of \(g(x) = \dfrac{x + 3}{x - 1}\) on \([3, 7]\).
stops.reflect: What is the same about every average rate of change problem, whatever the function looks like?

stages.desc: A practice check in the same format as the LF1 CheckIt exercise.

Part 2. Calculate the slope of each line.
(a) The line graphed below.[[graph:LC]](b) The line defined by the table

\(5\)\(1\)

stops.coldPlain: Part 1: Find the average rate of change of h(x) = 3x^2 - 4x on [-1, 3]. Part 2: Find the slope of (a) a graphed line, (b) the line in this table: x | y rows: (-10, -5), (-5, -3), (5, 1), (10, 3), (15, 5), (c) the line through (-5, 3) and (-2, -3).

stops.reflect: Which way of giving a line (graph, table, or points) is hardest for you, and why?
